title: Autonomous Rescue VTOL Aircraft
text:
April–September 2025 · Seoul National University · Team Bulnabi
I worked on the control software engineering team for a model aircraft with vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capabilities and visual target recognition for autonomous rescue. My work focused on perception and control software using YOLO and ROS 2 for target recognition and alignment control.
Our team placed in the top 7 of 37 teams at the 23rd Korea Robotic Aircraft Competition.

My contribution
As a member of the control software engineering team, I developed software connecting visual target recognition with aircraft alignment control:

Target recognition: used YOLO for the perception component of the autonomous rescue task.
Perception and control integration: developed ROS 2 software for target recognition and alignment control.

The aircraft design, construction, and competition result were a team effort. The photos below document the aircraft’s development and the separate quadcopter used for computer vision testing.

title: 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly
text:
December 2024–April 2025 · Seoul, Korea & Tucson, USA
I served as CFD Team Leader for Team Korea in the 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly competition. My responsibilities included airfoil selection and analysis of flight characteristics, using Python scripts to automate analysis with the Ansys Fluid API. I also conducted fluid–structure interaction analysis with Ansys Mechanical.
Read the final report (PDF)

title: 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly
text:
The aircraft and mission
Team Korea brought together students from Seoul National University, Gyeongsang National University, and Konkuk University. The team developed Beomgorae, a twin-motor carrier aircraft, and Gaori, a flying-wing X-1 test vehicle, for the competition’s flight and ground missions.
The design balanced payload capacity, flight speed, endurance, and the ability to carry and release the X-1 glider. The main aircraft used a low wing and a twin-boom H-tail. Aerodynamic analysis supported decisions about the wing geometry, airfoil, and mission configurations.

title: 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly
text:
My contribution
My role focused on the analysis that informed the aircraft design:

CFD team leadership: led the team’s CFD work on aerodynamic performance and flight characteristics.
Airfoil selection: evaluated candidate airfoils against lift and efficiency requirements.
Automated analysis: used Python and the Ansys Fluid API to support repeated aerodynamic analyses across aircraft configurations.
Fluid–structure interaction: used Ansys Mechanical to evaluate structural response to aerodynamic loading.

The aircraft, glider, manufacturing, and flight demonstrations were a wider team effort. The analysis figures below are extracted from Team Korea’s final report, which lists me on the aircraft analysis team in Section 2.1 (page 5).

title: 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly
text:
Airfoil selection
The report describes screening 1,648 airfoils from the UIUC database using XFLR5 at a Reynolds number of 700,000 and Mach 0.1. The selection considered lift capability and lift-to-drag ratio at the operating angles of attack.
The comparison below shows the symmetric S9027 alongside the cambered SG6043 and E216. SG6043 and E216 were retained for further sizing because they better met the lift and efficiency requirements. The final aircraft used E216.



Lift and lift-to-drag curves for the three selected airfoils.


Source: Figure 4.3, final report, page 18.

title: 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly
text:
CFD and aerodynamic performance

Configuration comparisons
The team used Ansys Fluent to evaluate the aircraft’s aerodynamic characteristics across mission configurations. The report describes a k–omega turbulence model, polyhedral meshing, and a Python script for running multiple configurations. The freestream velocity in the reported setup was 34 m/s.
The fuel tank, X-1 glider, and release hardware changed the external geometry, so the configurations were analyzed separately. The streamlines show how the surrounding flow changes with the added hardware.



Velocity streamlines around two aircraft mission configurations.


Source: Figure 4.23, final report, page 31.



Lift and drag coefficients across angles of attack for different mission configurations.


Source: Figure 4.24, final report, page 31.
The report identifies stall at approximately 12.5° in both analyzed configurations. The Mission 2 and 3 configurations produced slightly lower lift and higher drag than Mission 1, illustrating the aerodynamic cost of the additional mission hardware.


Checking the sizing model
Team Korea’s FORCAST sizing tool combined rapid lifting-surface analysis with a fuselage drag correction derived from Fluent. The comparison below checks its lift and drag predictions against Fluent for the same geometry.



Comparison of FORCAST and Ansys aerodynamic coefficients.


Source: Figure 4.8, final report, page 21.
The models followed similar trends within the reported operating range of −3° to 10°. The report also identifies a limit of the rapid vortex-lattice model: it cannot predict stall, making the Fluent comparison useful near the edge of the operating envelope.

title: 2025 AIAA Design/Build/Fly
section: From aerodynamic loads to structural response
text:
From aerodynamic loads to structural response
The structural analysis mapped Fluent pressure distributions onto the aircraft structure. The report considered an extreme load case up to 10g, assuming a linear elastic response without buckling, and examined stresses in the wing, fuselage, empennage, and internal supports.



Structural stress distributions on aircraft surfaces and internal supports.


Source: Figures 5.10–5.13, final report, page 38.
The report’s stress summary gives 85.48 MPa for the fuselage and main-wing composite surfaces and 14.91 MPa for the inner supports. These are simulation results under the stated assumptions. The report notes that physical testing remains necessary to account for manufacturing imperfections and fiber alignment.
Select any analysis figure to view it at full resolution.

title: Occlusion-Aware Drone Tracking
text:
AAE 568 · Team project
Hyunchang Kweon (Thomas), Chen-Yu Chang, and Gabriel Oliveira
Read the full report (PDF) View code on GitHub

title: Occlusion-Aware Drone Tracking
text:
The problem
Following a moving target requires more than staying close. When the target passes behind an obstacle, a drone can lose its line of sight even while remaining on a collision-free path. This project explores how a controller can balance visibility, tracking distance, obstacle avoidance, and control effort.
We studied this problem in a two-dimensional simulation with circular and elliptical obstacles. The drone maintains a fixed altitude, and the target follows a scripted path. The team compared an online SLSQP-based model predictive controller, an LQR-based controller, and an offline optimal-control benchmark based on Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle (PMP).

title: Occlusion-Aware Drone Tracking
text:
My contribution
As documented in the report’s individual contributions section (Section VI, page 12), I was responsible for:

Dynamics formulation: modeled the planar quadcopter and reduced its position dynamics to a double integrator using virtual acceleration inputs.
Simulation environment: built the base PyGame environment for testing obstacle layouts, target trajectories, and interchangeable controllers, with recording and logging support.
Occlusion-aware SLSQP-MPC: developed the controller formulation and explored three target trajectory predictors.
Evaluation: wrote the scripts for calculating metrics and comparing visibility, tracking performance, acceleration cost, and controller computation time.

title: Occlusion-Aware Drone Tracking
text:
Controller design
At each update, the controller predicts the target’s motion and optimizes a sequence of planar acceleration commands. It applies the first command, receives a new observation, and repeats the optimization.
The objective combines control effort, deviation from the desired tracking distance, and an occlusion penalty. Circular and elliptical obstacles are mapped into normalized coordinates so the controller can measure how closely the drone-to-target line of sight passes to an obstacle. An exponential penalty discourages configurations with poor visibility.
The optimization also imposes obstacle collision constraints, a minimum target separation throughout the horizon, a maximum target distance at the terminal step, and acceleration limits. Analytical cost gradients and constraint Jacobians are mapped from predicted positions to acceleration inputs for the SLSQP solver.

title: Occlusion-Aware Drone Tracking
text:
Three target predictors
The controller is evaluated with three ways of predicting the same target’s future motion. The attractive-field model changes the prediction, while the simulated target follows the scripted trajectory.


Constant velocity
Estimates velocity from consecutive position measurements and extrapolates it across the prediction horizon.



Drone tracking with the constant-velocity predictor.




Velocity and acceleration
Estimates both velocity and acceleration, with exponential moving averages to smooth the measurements.



Drone tracking with the velocity-and-acceleration predictor.




Attractive field
Adds an obstacle-attracted motion heuristic to anticipate a target that moves around obstacles to increase occlusion.



Drone tracking with the attractive-field predictor.




The blue marker is the drone, the red marker is the target, and the connecting line indicates their line of sight.

Results

Trajectories and time histories

Predictor comparison
The following values are reported in Table I, page 7 of the final report. Visibility values are scores, rather than percentages; the acceleration cost is the report’s squared-acceleration metric.

Constant velocity produced the smoothest response and the lowest acceleration cost. Velocity and acceleration achieved the highest average visibility score, alongside a rougher trajectory and larger computation-time spikes. Attractive field achieved the highest minimum visibility score, suggesting that anticipating obstacle-seeking target motion can improve the worst visibility encountered in this scenario.
These results use fixed controller weights in a scripted 2D scenario. They demonstrate a tradeoff between prediction complexity, visibility, and smoothness; broader weight tuning and more varied target behaviors are needed to establish how well the findings generalize.


Team comparisons
Chen-Yu Chang developed the LQR-based controller, including constraint and penalty terms. The report describes improvements in path consistency and visibility recovery through side-bias guidance and line-of-sight recovery logic.
Gabriel Oliveira developed the offline PMP benchmark, which uses the complete target trajectory before simulation. It provides a full-information reference for the online methods. In the reported comparison, it maintained tracking distance and line of sight but incurred a higher acceleration cost than the online MPC cases.

title: Occlusion-Aware Drone Tracking
text:
What I would explore next
A broader ablation of controller weights and predictor settings would help separate the effects of prediction from those of cost tuning. Other extensions identified in the report include richer models of evasive target motion and a higher-fidelity quadcopter model beyond the fixed-altitude 2D approximation.
